title: Fall and Recovery: Culiacán, the Humphrey Line, and the Moor's Pavane
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Culiacán, born in a bandmaster's house
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia's infobox gives birth name José Arcadio Limón, 12 January 1908, Culiacán; Wikidata Q785199 P19 = Culiacán, Sinaloa, from Britannica. The eldest-of-twelve figure and the musician father are in the article. The parents' names commonly printed, Florencio Limón and Francisca Traslaviña, appear in no reachable source: not en.wikipedia, not es.wikipedia, not Wikidata, where P22 and P25 are both empty. They are therefore not stated here.
stops.campa: José Arcadio Limón is born in Culiacán on the twelfth of January, eldest of twelve children in a house where music is work. His father conducts theater orchestras; the boy learns to sit through a rehearsal before he learns to read. The north of Mexico is already unquiet, and within seven years the family will be gone from it. No street, no house, no attending record survives, only the city and the date. What Culiacán gives him is not dance. It is the sound of an orchestra pit and a baton keeping time above it.
suggested_refs: Culiacán, Sinaloa, and the theater orchestras his father conducted

stops.name: Los Angeles, the family crosses north
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the destination (en.wikipedia; Britannica): the family emigrated in 1915 fleeing the Mexican Revolution and settled eventually in Los Angeles. Nothing finer is documented: no month, no port of entry, no first address. The date defaults to the first of January because the year is all the record carries.
stops.campa: In 1915 the Limón family crosses the border and settles in Los Angeles, one household among thousands the revolution pushes north that year. José is seven and has no English. The port of entry is not recorded, nor the month, nor the street they take. He will become an American citizen in 1946, thirty-one years after this crossing. The city holds him through boyhood, a high school in Lincoln Heights, and a false start at painting before it lets him go east.
suggested_refs: The 1915 northward emigration out of revolutionary Mexico into southern California

stops.name: Lincoln High School, Lincoln Heights
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction [R]: en.wikipedia attests that Limón graduated from Lincoln High School in Los Angeles and gives no year. The placement here is arithmetic on a 1908 birth and nothing else; no yearbook, registrar record or dated source was reached. Treat the year as a placement inside the adolescence, not as a documented date.
stops.campa: At Lincoln High School in Lincoln Heights he takes his American schooling, building English on top of Spanish as he goes. The year he finishes is not documented in any source reached; it is placed by arithmetic on a birth date and nothing more. Those who remember him describe a serious boy, watchful, carrying the weight of eleven younger brothers and sisters. Nothing here points toward a studio floor three thousand miles east. He draws constantly through those years, and he means to be a painter.
suggested_refs: Lincoln High School, Lincoln Heights, Los Angeles

stops.name: The Vermont Avenue campus, the art major
stops.date_confidence: the enrollment and the major are attested (en.wikipedia: Limón attended UCLA as an art major intending to become a painter); the 1926 start year is unsourced and tagged [R]. The pin is corrected: UCLA's original campus was the Vermont Avenue site, now Los Angeles City College, at 34.0870, -118.2929, and the university moved to Westwood in 1929. An earlier pass pinned this 1.5 km south, near Vermont and Beverly.
stops.campa: He enrolls at the university's Vermont Avenue campus as an art major, meaning to be a painter. The buildings will become Los Angeles City College once the university moves west to Westwood in 1929; for now they are UCLA, and Limón draws in them. He is good enough to believe painting is his future, and those who knew him then recall an interest in the human figure in motion rather than in landscape. He leaves without a degree. In 1928 he takes the train east with a portfolio and no money.
suggested_refs: The old UCLA Vermont Avenue campus, occupied by Los Angeles City College after the 1929 move to Westwood

stops.name: 2 West 13th Street, the School of Design
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move and the institution (en.wikipedia: in 1928 Limón moved to New York City to study painting at the New York School of Design). The street address is [R]: 2 West 13th Street is commonly given for the school and was not confirmed in any source reached this pass. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: At the New York School of Design he studies painting in a city that owes an unknown twenty-year-old nothing. He sketches and counts what he has left to live on. Within twelve months he will stop drawing altogether, and nobody teaching him has any reason to expect it. The address commonly given for the school is 2 West 13th Street, which no source reached this pass confirms. The enrollment itself is documented and the year is firm. The city is fourteen months from the crash.
suggested_refs: The New York School of Design, Manhattan, and its commonly cited West 13th Street address

stops.name: Manhattan, the concert that ended the painting
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the effect (en.wikipedia: discouraged with painting, Limón saw a concert by Harald Kreutzberg and Yvonne Georgi and was inspired to become a dancer). The venue is a flat gap; the pin is the Broadway theater district as a placeholder. Attribution contradiction flagged and not resolved: the quotation carried here is verbatim on the Pacific Northwest Ballet repertory page, but PNB names neither Kreutzberg nor Georgi and frames it as his reaction to the first dance program he saw after arriving in New York in 1928.
stops.campa: In 1929 Limón goes to a dance concert in a New York theater and comes out of it finished with painting. He is twenty-one, older than the beginners he is about to stand beside in a studio. The record says he saw the German dancers Harald Kreutzberg and Yvonne Georgi; the passage in which he describes the evening names no one at all, and calls it simply the first dance program he attended in the city. Which of the two accounts is right, and which house he sat in that night, nothing reached says.
stops.quote: What I saw simply and irrevocably changed my life. I saw the dance as a vision of ineffable power. A man could, with dignity and towering majesty, dance... dance as Michelangelo's visions dance and as the music of Bach dances.
stops.quote_source: José Limón, on the first dance program he saw in New York, quoted on the Pacific Northwest Ballet repertory page for José Limón; the page gives no further citation and names no dancers
sources: Pacific Northwest Ballet, repertory page for José Limón
suggested_refs: The 1929 New York recitals of Harald Kreutzberg and Yvonne Georgi

stops.name: Chelsea, the Humphrey-Weidman school
stops.date_confidence: the enrollment and the teachers are attested (en.wikipedia: Limón enrolled at the Humphrey-Weidman School and studied under Doris Humphrey and Charles Weidman). The month is not recorded and June is a placement inside the year. The studio address is [R]: no street number was found, and the pin is Chelsea, where the school is conventionally placed. Humphrey and Weidman's Denishawn origin is attested in en.wikipedia, 'Doris Humphrey'.
stops.campa: He enrolls at the Humphrey-Weidman school and puts himself under Doris Humphrey and Charles Weidman, who had broken from Denishawn, the company of Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn, barely a year before. He is older than the other beginners and moves like a man not yet certain his body will obey him. Humphrey does not see a star at first. She sees, within a few classes, someone who takes correction instead of resisting it, and she begins building a vocabulary of fall and recovery onto him that will take twelve years.
stops.quote: you can hide behind words and facial expression
stops.quote_source: Doris Humphrey to her students, on the other arts, reported in José Limón, An Unfinished Memoir, p. 56; only this clause is traceable as quoted matter, and the sentence often printed after it is a later reviewer's paraphrase
sources: racheloriol.wordpress.com, 23 March 2016, review of An Unfinished Memoir
suggested_refs: The Humphrey-Weidman school, Manhattan, and its descent from the Denishawn company of Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn

stops.name: Broadway, the first appearance and the Little Group
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1930 (en.wikipedia: first Broadway performance; first choreography, Etude in D Minor, a duet with Letitia Ide). The Little Group is attested in the same 1930 passage, which reads that Limón recruited Ide and schoolmates Eleanor King and Ernestine Stodelle; the 1931 date carried in earlier passes is not in the source and is dropped, the founding rendered c. 1930 and tagged [R]. The theater of the Broadway debut is a gap, and the pin is the theater district.
stops.campa: Two years out of art school he makes his first Broadway appearance and choreographs his first dance, Etude in D Minor, a duet with Letitia Ide. In the same season he recruits Ide and two schoolmates, Eleanor King and Ernestine Stodelle, into an independent offshoot they call the Little Group. He had been a painter in 1928. The theater of his Broadway debut is not recorded, and neither is the room the Little Group worked in, nor how long the four of them kept it going.
suggested_refs: Etude in D Minor, the first Limón choreography, and the Little Group of Ide, King and Stodelle

stops.name: Music Box Theatre, As Thousands Cheer
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia states that from 1932 to 1933 Limón made two more Broadway appearances, in the revue Americana and in Irving Berlin's As Thousands Cheer, choreographed by Charles Weidman. As Thousands Cheer opened 30 September 1933 at the Music Box Theatre; Americana had opened in October 1932. Earlier passes collapsed both shows into a single 1932 date, which is wrong for the second.
stops.campa: At the Music Box on West 45th Street he dances in Irving Berlin's revue As Thousands Cheer, choreographed by Charles Weidman, with Ethel Waters billed above him. Broadway pays and the concert studio does not, not reliably, and the Depression makes the arithmetic simple. He crosses between the two worlds for over a decade. A year earlier he had appeared in the revue Americana, which opened in October 1932. The two engagements are routinely collapsed into a single date. They are two seasons and two houses apart.
suggested_refs: As Thousands Cheer, Music Box Theatre, opened 30 September 1933, choreography by Charles Weidman

stops.name: Bennington College, the Fellow
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (en.wikipedia: Limón was named a Bennington Fellow in 1937). The month is a placement inside the summer session. Two corrections carried: the fellowship is 1937, not a span beginning 1934, which is the founding year of the Bennington School of the Dance under Martha Hill; and the campus pin is 42.9247, -73.2367, inherited byte-identical from martha_graham.journey.json, an earlier pass having pinned Bennington village 3.5 km off.
stops.campa: Named a Bennington Fellow at the summer school Martha Hill founded in 1934, Limón spends his weeks on a Vermont campus where American modern dance argues with itself in close quarters. Humphrey, Weidman and Hanya Holm teach the same six weeks, technique set against technique, and the fall-and-recovery principle he has been given in New York is tested here daily against every other answer in the field. He is twenty-nine and has choreographed nothing anyone yet calls major.
suggested_refs: The Bennington School of the Dance, founded 1934 by Martha Hill, active to 1942

stops.name: Mills College, Danzas Mexicanas
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, the work and the place (en.wikipedia: Danzas Mexicanas, Limón's first major independent choreography, premiered at the Bennington Festival, held that year at Mills College). The August date is a placement inside the festival season; no premiere date was recovered. The quotation is from An Unfinished Memoir, reached only through the Jacob's Pillow essay, never against a copy of the book.
stops.campa: The Bennington Festival moves west for a season to Mills College, and on that stage Limón premieres Danzas Mexicanas, his first major work of his own. It is built on figures out of Mexican history, and the revolution in it is not an abstraction to him: it is why the family left Culiacán when he was seven. Oakland is the farthest west he has worked since he left Los Angeles for good. He is thirty-one, and critics now write about him as a choreographer. He has no company and will not have one for seven years.
stops.quote: the cruel, heroic, and at the same time beautiful story of my native land has long held a singular fascination for me. It is never entirely absent from my thinking.
stops.quote_source: José Limón, An Unfinished Memoir, quoted in 'Reflections on José Limón,' Jacob's Pillow Dance Interactive
sources: Jacob's Pillow Dance Interactive, 'Reflections on José Limón'
suggested_refs: Danzas Mexicanas, premiered at the 1939 Bennington Festival at Mills College, Oakland

stops.name: Broadhurst Theatre, Keep Off the Grass
stops.date_confidence: attested and corrected: Keep Off the Grass, with choreography by George Balanchine, opened 23 May 1940 at the Broadhurst Theatre and ran 44 performances (en.wikipedia, 'Keep Off the Grass'). Earlier passes dated Limón's appearance 1944, a reading produced by the ambiguous sentence in the Limón article that follows the 1939 Mills paragraph. The corrected date places this engagement before Rosalinda, not after it.
stops.campa: At the Broadhurst on West 44th Street he returns to Broadway as a featured dancer in Keep Off the Grass, choreographed by George Balanchine. It opens on the twenty-third of May and runs forty-four performances. The date matters because the standard telling moves this engagement four years forward, into 1944, on the strength of one ambiguous sentence; it belongs here, before the war and before Rosalinda. Limón is thirty-two, working for a ballet choreographer in a commercial house.
suggested_refs: Keep Off the Grass, Broadhurst Theatre, 23 May 1940, choreography by George Balanchine

stops.name: San Francisco, marrying Pauline Lawrence
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested in en.wikipedia, 'José Limón,' cited to Limón 1998, p. 108. The place is corrected: en.wikipedia, 'Pauline Lawrence,' gives 'Marriage: October 3, 1941 in San Francisco to José Limón,' where earlier passes said New York. The correction fits the year, in which Limón had left the Humphrey-Weidman company and was working on the West Coast with May O'Donnell. No ceremony site within the city is recorded.
stops.campa: He has left the Humphrey-Weidman company and is working on the West Coast with the dancer May O'Donnell when he marries Pauline Lawrence in San Francisco on the third of October. The wedding is routinely placed in New York; it was not. She had been the Humphrey-Weidman company's pianist, costumer and manager, and from this date she is his closest collaborator, designing the costumes, running the tours and keeping the books of a company that does not yet exist. No ceremony site inside the city is recorded.
suggested_refs: Pauline Lawrence Limón, pianist, costumer and company manager, married 3 October 1941 in San Francisco

stops.name: Broadway, Rosalinda and the last curtain
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the fact (en.wikipedia: Limón's final Broadway appearance, in Balanchine's Rosalinda). No month, no theater and no run length were recovered, so the pin is the theater district and the date defaults to the first of January. The draft that follows is dated April 1943 in the same article.
stops.campa: He makes his last Broadway appearance in Balanchine's Rosalinda, and the commercial theater is finished with him and he with it. Thirteen years separate this stage from the first Broadway job he took as a beginner out of Humphrey's ensemble. The revues had fed him through the Depression and had never been the work. He is thirty-five years old. In April of the same year the United States Army drafts him, and the choosing is taken out of his hands entirely.
suggested_refs: Rosalinda, Limón's final Broadway engagement, choreography by George Balanchine

stops.name: Washington, the Army years
stops.date_confidence: the draft is attested for April 1943 and the citizenship for 1946 (en.wikipedia). Everything between is a gap: no camp, no unit, no theater of service, and the Special Services assignment itself is [R]. The pin at Washington, D.C. is an admitted placeholder and is not a place Limón is known to have stood. Stated as a gap rather than filled.
stops.campa: Drafted in April 1943, Limón spends three years in uniform, assigned in part to Special Services, the branch that made entertainment for troops. Where he was stationed is not recorded in anything reached: no camp, no unit, no theater of service. Three years of an otherwise well-documented life go dark here, and the location given for them is a placeholder rather than any place he is known to have stood. He leaves the Army in 1946 and becomes an American citizen the same year.
suggested_refs: United States Army Special Services, 1943-1946, postings undocumented

stops.name: New York, the citizenship and the company
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year on both counts (en.wikipedia: Limón attained American citizenship in 1946 and formed the José Limón Dance Company with Doris Humphrey as artistic director and himself as principal dancer and choreographer). No month is given for either, and no founding address for the company survives in anything reached, so the canonical New York pin is used.
stops.campa: In the year he takes American citizenship, Limón forms a company and does an unusual thing with it: he installs Doris Humphrey as artistic director and keeps for himself only the parts of principal dancer and choreographer. He is thirty-eight and months out of the Army, and no first address for the company survives in anything reached. His teacher, who can no longer perform, will shape the repertory for the next twelve years, deciding what the company dances and what it does not.
suggested_refs: The founding arrangement of the José Limón Dance Company, 1946, with Humphrey as artistic director

stops.name: Bennington College, the company's debut
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the place (en.wikipedia: the new company gave its formal debut performance at Bennington College). The August date is a placement inside the summer season; no performance date and no program were recovered. Campus pin inherited byte-identical from martha_graham.journey.json.
stops.campa: The new company gives its formal debut on the Bennington campus where Limón had been a Fellow nine years earlier, in front of the summer audience that knows better than any other in the country what it is looking at. Humphrey directs from the wings. Pauline Lawrence has made the costumes, and the dancers are few. The program of that first night is not recorded in any source reached. The place is recorded, and the place is the same Vermont field it was in 1937.
suggested_refs: The 1946 debut season of the José Limón Dance Company at Bennington College

stops.name: Belasco Theatre, Day on Earth
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, the theater and the work (en.wikipedia: the company debuted in New York at the Belasco Theatre dancing Doris Humphrey's Day on Earth, choreographed for Limón after arthritis ended her performing). No month or exact date was recovered. The New York Times notice calling him the finest male dancer of his time is reported by the same article and was not read in the original.
stops.campa: The company takes New York at the Belasco on West 44th Street, dancing Day on Earth, which Humphrey choreographed for Limón after arthritis ended her own performing. It is the first time his name stands on a marquee as the thing being sold rather than as a featured dancer in somebody else's show. The New York Times calls him the finest male dancer of his time; that notice is reported at second hand and was not read in the original. Pauline Lawrence runs the production from the wings. He is thirty-nine.
suggested_refs: Day on Earth, choreographed by Doris Humphrey for Limón, Belasco Theatre, 1947

stops.name: Connecticut College, the first festival summer
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the place (en.wikipedia: the company first appeared at the Connecticut College American Dance Festival in 1948, which became a recurring home for Limón's premieres). The August date is a placement inside the festival season and is not documented.
stops.campa: The company appears for the first time at the American Dance Festival on the Connecticut College campus in New London, the summer gathering that inherits from Bennington the work of assembling the whole field in one place each August. Limón comes now as a company director rather than a fellow among fellows; the difference is two years old. The Festival will take his premieres for the next two decades, beginning the following August, and New London becomes the place where the field comes to see what he has made since last summer.
suggested_refs: The Connecticut College American Dance Festival, New London, successor to the Bennington summers

stops.name: Palmer Auditorium, The Moor's Pavane
stops.date_confidence: attested: the premiere of The Moor's Pavane at the Connecticut College American Dance Festival on 17 August 1949, set to Purcell, based on Othello, winner of a Dance Magazine Award (en.wikipedia, 'The Moor's Pavane' and 'José Limón'). The pin is the Connecticut College campus; Palmer Auditorium is the campus's festival house and its identification as the specific room is [R].
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of August, at the Connecticut College festival, Limón premieres The Moor's Pavane: four dancers, a court dance set to Purcell, a handkerchief, and the whole plot of Othello without one word of Shakespeare spoken. He dances the Moor himself. Weight is given to gravity and taken back from it, which is what Humphrey put into him starting in 1929 and what the four bodies are doing the whole way through. It takes a Dance Magazine Award, never leaves the repertory, and is danced now by companies that never saw him alive.
suggested_refs: The Moor's Pavane, 17 August 1949, music of Henry Purcell, after Shakespeare's Othello

stops.name: Paris, the first American company in Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact and the year (en.wikipedia: the company toured Paris in 1950, the first American modern dance company to perform in Europe, sharing the engagement with Ruth Page's company). The spring dating is loose and the April date is a placement. The theater is a flat gap: an earlier pass speculatively placed it at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, which nothing reached confirms, so the canonical Paris pin is used instead.
stops.campa: The company crosses to Paris in the spring, the first American modern dance troupe to perform in Europe, sharing the engagement with Ruth Page's company. Paris knows ballet. It does not know a body that falls on purpose and catches itself, and it has never watched a Mexican-born American dance Othello to Purcell. Which theater took them is not recorded in anything reached, and neither is what the audience made of it. The city is as close as the record gets.
suggested_refs: The 1950 European tour of the José Limón Dance Company with Ruth Page's company

stops.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes, six works in Mexico
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, the invitation and the output (en.wikipedia: invited by Mexico City's Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes in 1951, Limón created six new works). No month, no titles and no performance dates were recovered; the pin is the Palacio de Bellas Artes as the Instituto's house. The Berg quotation is verbatim in the Jacob's Pillow essay; the hedge carried in an earlier pass, treating it as that essay's paraphrase, was wrong.
stops.campa: The Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes brings him to Mexico City, and in one engagement he makes six new works on the soil his family fled in 1915. He is forty-three, working inside his country's chief arts institution rather than running from its wars. Culiacán is nine hundred miles north of this theater and a lifetime from the boy who left it. No source reached calls the return emotional. The record says only that the work was fast and that there was a great deal of it.
stops.quote: Limón, already feeling a conflict between his Mexican and Spanish heritage, saw his choreography as a way to embed his ethnicity within the evolving aesthetic of American modern dance.
stops.quote_source: Shelly C. Berg, in Patricia Seed, ed., José Limón and La Malinche: The Dancer and the Dance (University of Texas Press, 2008), quoted in 'Reflections on José Limón,' Jacob's Pillow Dance Interactive
sources: Jacob's Pillow Dance Interactive, 'Reflections on José Limón'
suggested_refs: The six works made for the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes, Mexico City, 1951

stops.name: 120 Claremont Avenue, the Juilliard faculty
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (en.wikipedia: Limón joined the dance faculty of the Juilliard School in 1951); the September date is a placement at the start of an academic year and is not documented. Juilliard stood at 120 Claremont Avenue until its Lincoln Center move of October 1969. Pin inherited byte-identical from jennifer_muller.journey.json. The Delsarte rung of the lineage is [R], the queue's framing rather than a claim Limón is recorded making.
stops.campa: He joins the dance faculty at Juilliard, then still at 120 Claremont Avenue in Morningside Heights, next door to the Union Theological Seminary. Here the vocabulary becomes a curriculum: fall and recovery taught as a grammar rather than copied as a style, to students who will carry it into companies he never leads. The line behind it, as the record reconstructs it and not as he ever claimed it, runs back through Humphrey to the Denishawn stage and behind that to Delsarte's system of expression.
suggested_refs: Juilliard at 120 Claremont Avenue, Morningside Heights, before the 1969 Lincoln Center move

stops.name: New York, The Emperor Jones
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the source play (en.wikipedia: Limón choreographed The Emperor Jones, after Eugene O'Neill, in 1956). The premiere venue is a gap, so the canonical New York pin is used and the date defaults to the first of January. The quotation is dated 1958 and is a later defense of the work, cross-checked on two independent fetches of the Wikipedia article, both returning identical wording with a citation marker.
stops.campa: He choreographs The Emperor Jones out of Eugene O'Neill's play, working the way he prefers to work, staging literature through movement rather than through mime. The premiere venue is not recorded. The piece draws an argument he answers directly two years later, defending the blackface he used in it as a matter of art rather than of usage, in a sentence that reads now as of its decade and did not read that way to him. The company keeps the work in repertory. He is forty-eight.
stops.quote: Emperor Jones was first of all a work of art, and I hoped a good one, and that even if it were in defiance of prevalent political and social usages, no one would or could prohibit its performance.
stops.quote_source: José Limón, 1958 statement defending his use of blackface in The Emperor Jones, quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'José Limón'
sources: Jacob's Pillow Dance Interactive, 'Reflections on José Limón'
suggested_refs: The Emperor Jones, after Eugene O'Neill, and James Moreno's reading of Limón's racial positioning in The Oxford Handbook of Dance and Politics

stops.name: New York, the seasons with Pauline Koner
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact without a fine date (en.wikipedia dates the close artistic partnership with the dancer Pauline Koner to 1958 and names no individual works); the second Dance Magazine Award is attested for 1957. The date defaults to the first of January and the canonical New York pin is used, no studio or theater being recorded.
stops.campa: Through these seasons Limón builds a run of works around the dancer Pauline Koner, whose place in the company is close enough to the center that the partnership is entered in the record as a fact in its own right. In 1957 he had taken a second Dance Magazine Award, eight years after the first. The company is touring internationally now, carrying his choreography and Humphrey's together, and the arrangement he set up in 1946, the teacher directing the pupil's company, is in its twelfth year.
suggested_refs: The Limón and Pauline Koner collaborations of the later 1950s

stops.name: New York, Doris Humphrey dies
stops.date_confidence: attested: Doris Humphrey died 29 December 1958 (en.wikipedia, 'Doris Humphrey'), after which Limón assumed the artistic directorship of his own company (en.wikipedia, 'José Limón'). The canonical New York pin is used; no place of death is asserted here. The memoir quotation is at one remove, through a 2016 review, and the trailing ellipsis carried in earlier passes is spurious: the sentence is complete as quoted.
stops.campa: Doris Humphrey dies on the twenty-ninth of December, and Limón becomes sole artistic director of the company that has carried his name since 1946. He has worked under her for twenty-nine years: first as her student, then as her principal dancer, then as the choreographer she directed. Day on Earth, Night Spell, Ruins and Visions and the Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías stay in the repertory, and he keeps them there. He is fifty, and there is no longer anyone above him.
stops.quote: The choreographic genius of Doris Humphrey was an affirmation of order and clarity.
stops.quote_source: José Limón, An Unfinished Memoir, p. 55, quoted on racheloriol.wordpress.com, 23 March 2016
sources: racheloriol.wordpress.com, review of An Unfinished Memoir

stops.name: Delacorte Theater, the Shakespeare Festival
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the occasion (en.wikipedia: the company performed in Central Park for the opening of the New York Shakespeare Festival's public theater season in 1962). Correction carried: the Delacorte opened 18 June 1962 with The Merchant of Venice, so this falls in the theater's inaugural season, not four years after its building as an earlier pass had it. The June date is a placement. The source's word 'returned' implies earlier Festival appearances at pre-Delacorte sites, undocumented in anything reached.
stops.campa: The company opens the New York Shakespeare Festival's public season in Central Park, in the Delacorte's first summer; the house had opened in June with The Merchant of Venice. Free, outdoors, in a park, for whoever walks up: it is a larger audience than any dance festival has put in front of him. He is fifty-four. The record says the company returned to Central Park, which implies earlier Festival appearances at sites nobody reached this pass has documented.
suggested_refs: The Delacorte Theater, Central Park, opened 18 June 1962

stops.name: New York, Jennifer Muller enters the company
stops.date_confidence: attested: a 1981 New York Times profile and the Limón Dance Company's own posting both give her as principal in the company from 1963 to 1971 (jennifer_muller.journey.json). No month is recorded and no company address is documented, so the canonical New York pin is used, byte-identical to hers. Contradiction inherited and not adjudicated: Muller's own biography says nine years, and 1963 to 1971 is eight.
stops.campa: Jennifer Muller joins the company at eighteen and stays a principal through 1971, learning a body that falls and recovers, weight surrendered to gravity and taken back from it. She will found her own company in 1974 and carry the vocabulary into it, setting work as far south as Buenos Aires. Limón is fifty-five and has taught at Juilliard for twelve years, where she trained as well. Her own account says nine years in his company; the company's posting says 1963 to 1971, which is eight.

segments.name: The Institutional Years and the Last Stage

stops.name: Lincoln Center, the American Dance Theater
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year on both counts (en.wikipedia: Limón received the Capezio Dance Award in 1964 and was appointed artistic director of the American Dance Theater at Lincoln Center the same year). No month is given for either. How long the American Dance Theater lasted, and what it produced, are not documented in anything reached.
stops.campa: He is appointed artistic director of the American Dance Theater at Lincoln Center, and takes the Capezio Dance Award in the same year. The post is not his own company: it is an institutional chair, meant to represent American modern dance at the newest and most expensive arts complex in the country. A man born in Sinaloa in 1908, when no such art form was organized anywhere, is put at the administrative top of it at fifty-six. How long the American Dance Theater lasted is not on the record reached.

stops.name: New York, the statement of belief
stops.date_confidence: attested for the text and the volume: Limón's statement appears in Selma Jeanne Cohen, ed., The Modern Dance: Seven Statements of Belief (Wesleyan University Press, 1966), quoted on the University of Washington Department of Dance faculty page for Limón. The Cohen volume itself was not read; the quotation is at one remove. No place or month of composition is recorded, so the canonical New York pin is used and the date is the publication year.
stops.campa: Asked with six other choreographers to say what he believes, Limón puts his descent in writing and names the people he takes it from: Isadora Duncan first, then the American impetus as he sees it in Doris Humphrey and Martha Graham, and the conviction that dance can carry the sublimity of tragedy. He is fifty-eight. It is the clearest statement he ever makes about where he stands and whose work he considers himself continuing. Selma Jeanne Cohen's volume appears in 1966; the pages were read here at one remove, through a university faculty page quoting them.
stops.quote: I view myself as a disciple and follower of Isadora Duncan, and the American impetus as exemplified by Doris Humphrey and Martha Graham, and by their vision of the dance as an art capable of the sublimity of tragedy and the Dionysian ecstasies.
stops.quote_source: José Limón, in Selma Jeanne Cohen, ed., The Modern Dance: Seven Statements of Belief (Wesleyan University Press, 1966), quoted on the University of Washington Department of Dance faculty page
sources: University of Washington Department of Dance, faculty page for José Limón

stops.name: Washington National Cathedral, dancing in the nave
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the venue (en.wikipedia: the company performed at Washington National Cathedral in 1967 and received a National Endowment for the Arts grant the same year). stops.campa: The company dances in the nave of Washington National Cathedral, a Gothic church built for choirs and state funerals rather than for a technique founded on falling. Stone carries sound differently than a proscenium does; the dancers work in it anyway. The same year the National Endowment for the Arts, then two years old, makes the company a grant, and the federal government begins treating dance as a line worth defending in a budget. The program of that evening is not recorded.

The boy who crossed the border at seven, in a household running from a revolution, dances in the residence of the President of the United States at fifty-nine, for the head of a second state as well. stops.name: New York, the Foundation incorporated
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (en.wikipedia: the José Limón Foundation was incorporated in 1968 to sustain the company and its repertory). No month, no filing date and no office address were recovered, so the canonical New York pin is used. The Limón Institute, formed in 1985 to hold the technique, repertory and archives, is a separate later body.
stops.campa: Limón incorporates the José Limón Foundation, a legal body to hold the company, the repertory and whatever comes after. The papers are filed in New York. He is sixty and does not describe it as a provision against his own death; the cancer is two years off and undiagnosed. The Foundation is what will keep The Moor's Pavane onstage into a century he does not see, danced by people who never met him, and it will be given a National Medal of Arts forty years from now.

stops.name: Brooklyn Academy of Music, the last performances
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, the venue and the two works (en.wikipedia: Limón gave his final onstage performances in 1969, dancing in The Traitor and The Moor's Pavane at the Brooklyn Academy of Music). No month or performance date was recovered. The quoted statement is a written one of 1965, placed here as a gloss on the performing career rather than as words spoken at this event.
stops.campa: At the Brooklyn Academy of Music he dances in public for the last time, in The Traitor and in The Moor's Pavane, the Othello he made twenty years earlier at Connecticut College. He is sixty-one, and the cancer is a year off from being found. The performing career that opened on a Broadway stage in 1930, in a body he was still learning to trust, closes here. He does not stop working; he choreographs and teaches for three more years. Whether he went out that night knowing it was the last time, nothing reached says.
stops.quote: I try to compose works that are involved with man's basic tragedy and the grandeur of his spirit. I want to dig beneath empty formalisms, displays of technical virtuosity, and the slick surface; to probe the human entity for the powerful, often crude beauty of the gesture that speaks of man's humanity. I reach for demons, saints, martyrs, apostates, fools, and other impassioned visions.
stops.quote_source: José Limón, written statement, 1965, quoted on the University of Washington Department of Dance faculty page
sources: University of Washington Department of Dance, faculty page for José Limón
suggested_refs: The Traitor and The Moor's Pavane, Brooklyn Academy of Music, 1969, Limón's last appearances as a dancer

stops.name: New York, the diagnosis
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the disease (en.wikipedia: Limón was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 1970). No month, no physician, no hospital is recorded, and no place is given, so the canonical New York pin is used. Note that Wikidata Q785199 gives kidney disease as cause of death, contradicting the prostate cancer of both the Limón Foundation summaries and es.wikipedia; the contradiction is recorded, not resolved.
stops.campa: Prostate cancer is diagnosed in 1970. He is sixty-two, a year off the stage, still teaching at Juilliard and still making work. Pauline Lawrence, who has managed everything unglamorous about his career since 1941, is herself within eighteen months of her death. Nothing in the record describes how either of them took the news. The diagnosis appears in the biographies as a bare year with no scene attached to it, and the company keeps touring around it.

stops.name: Stockton, the farm above the Delaware
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia, 'Pauline Lawrence,' gives her death on 16 July 1971 at the property near Stockton, New Jersey, a former dairy farm the couple bought in 1948 and renovated into a house and a studio. This is the residence commonly and wrongly placed at Flemington, 13 km northeast. The televised solo Limón filmed for CBS during his illness is attested without a date and is a gap.
stops.campa: Pauline Lawrence Limón dies on the sixteenth of July at the converted dairy farm above the Delaware near Stockton, which the two of them bought in 1948 and rebuilt into a house and a studio. Thirty years of marriage, and thirty years of the company's costumes, tours and accounts, end in the same rooms. He stays on at the farm. He has seventeen months left, and spends part of them choreographing and filming a solo for television at CBS, on a date nobody reached has recorded.

stops.name: Flemington, the death in Hunterdon County
stops.date_confidence: the date and the age are firm (en.wikipedia lead: 12 January 1908 to 2 December 1972; he died of cancer at the age of 64). The place is an unresolved three-way contradiction, flagged and not adjudicated: en.wikipedia's infobox leaves death_place blank; Wikidata Q785199 gives New York City with cause 'kidney disease,' both Freebase- and IMDb-derived and the weakest of the three; es.wikipedia gives Flemington, New Jersey, with prostate cancer. The couple's actual home was near Stockton, 13 km southwest. Pinned at Flemington after es.wikipedia, with the conflict recorded here.
stops.campa: José Limón dies on the second of December, aged sixty-four, in Hunterdon County, New Jersey. Where exactly is a contradiction the sources have never settled: the Spanish record says Flemington, the English one leaves the place blank, and a database says New York City and names the wrong disease. The farm he actually lived on stands thirteen kilometers southwest, near Stockton. Sixty-four years, from a bandmaster's house in Culiacán to a county in New Jersey with three answers in it.
suggested_refs: The unresolved place of death: Flemington per es.wikipedia, New York City per Wikidata, blank in en.wikipedia, the farm near Stockton

stops.name: New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, the collection
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (en.wikipedia: the José Limón Collection was donated to the New York Public Library Dance Collection in 1973, the year after his death), and for the 1996 retrospective exhibition of Limón material at the same library. No month or accession date was recovered for either.
stops.campa: The José Limón Collection goes to the New York Public Library Dance Collection at Lincoln Center the year after his death: films, scores, notes, the paper record of forty-three working years. The donation is made while every dancer who worked with him is still alive, and what those dancers know does not go into the boxes with the paper. Notation, film and reconstruction get part of it and lose the rest, which is the standing problem of an art made out of bodies. The Library mounts a retrospective of the material in 1996.
